extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate/graduate mathematics students and mathematically literate readers interested in maxima/minima and variational problems
extracted.subtask_description: Techniques, existence conditions, and geometric constructions for maxima/minima problems (e.g., Steiner's problem, shortest networks, AM-GM, least squares), with emphasis on when extrema exist and how to characterize them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Light triangle as stationary-length triangle
rubrics_metrics.description: A light triangle ABC may be characterized by the fact that its length has a stationary value; this value may be a minimum with respect to all three points A, B, C, or may be a minimum with respect to some points and a maximum with respect to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify light triangles by which coordinates give minima/maxima. The existence argument yields at least 2^3 = 8 light triangles because for each of the three points either a maximum or a minimum is possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use reflection/optical properties to classify trajectories (ergodicity examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: For billiard problems and light rays in bounded domains one must analyze reflections; e.g., in an ellipse, rays through a focus reflect through the other focus, and rays not through a focus remain tangent to some confocal conic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply geometric reflection properties (especially of conics) to determine invariant sets of trajectories and hence decide (non-)ergodicity; use these dynamical/optical characterizations as part of extremal reasoning when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steiner problem — 120° characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: If in triangle ABC all angles are less than 120°, then the point P minimizing a + b + c (sum of distances to the vertices) is the point from which each of the three sides AB, BC, CA subtends an angle of 120°; if one angle (say C) is ≥ 120°, the minimum point P coincides with that vertex (C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct P by intersecting appropriate arcs: draw circles on two sides that subtend 120° arcs and take the intersection of the two shorter arcs. Proof uses extremum analysis: either P is a vertex or lies at such a 120° point; rule out other configurations by comparing sums of distances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive circle-arc method for Steiner point
rubrics_metrics.description: To find P (if it exists inside the triangle), draw circles K1, K2 on two sides such that the given side subtends arcs of 120°; P is the intersection of the two shorter arcs (if they intersect inside the triangle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish shorter vs longer arcs: on the shorter arc AC subtends 120°, on the longer arc 60°. Use intersection of shorter arcs to ensure the three angles at P add to 360° and are each 120°.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complementary minimization problems (a + b - c etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Complementary problems arise (e.g., minimize a + b − c); such problems may be solved by similar constructions but yield different characteristic angle patterns (e.g., P' where the larger side appears under 120° and the two smaller sides under 60°).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous geometric constructions and angle-characterizations apply; analyze which combinations of ± signs in the target expression change which geometric configuration gives the extremum.

rubrics_metrics.name: General street-network (Steiner tree) characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: For n given points, the shortest connected system of straight segments (Steiner tree) so any two given points can be joined has multiple intersections where three segments meet at angles of 120°; there are at most n−2 such multiple intersections, and solutions need not be unique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use local 120° junction rule to build candidate networks; check arrangement-dependent degeneracies (intersections may degenerate to given points). For symmetric configurations (e.g., square) expect multiple equivalent solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extrema produce inequalities (derive inequalities via extremum problems)
rubrics_metrics.description: A maximum (or minimum) solution of a problem yields an inequality expressing that the variable quantity is at most (or at least) the extremal value; such inequalities often have independent interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate geometric or optimization solutions into algebraic inequalities; example: among rectangles of fixed perimeter the square maximizes area leading to AM-GM inequality for two variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arithmetic mean ≥ geometric mean (AM-GM) via extremum
rubrics_metrics.description: For positive x,y with fixed sum 2m, the product xy is maximal when x = y = m, yielding the inequality √(xy) ≤ (x+y)/2; in general for n positives, the geometric mean ≤ arithmetic mean with equality only when all variables are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove by setting up product maximization under fixed sum, or by algebraic manipulations (introduce m and d), or via geometric tangent-of-hyperbola picture; use replacement argument to equalize two unequal summands to increase product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of least squares — arithmetic mean minimizes sum of squares
rubrics_metrics.description: Given readings x1,...,xn, the arithmetic mean m minimizes the sum of squared deviations Σ(u − xi)^2 over u; in regression-like problems choose parameters (e.g., a,b in y = ax + b) to minimize sum of squared vertical deviations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive by expanding squares and using definition of mean (cross terms vanish). Use this least-squares principle as a guiding variational method for fitting models; the resulting minimization is a finite-dimensional extremum problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish constructive proofs vs. existence-then-characterize proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Two logical methods: (1) constructive demonstration that a candidate attains a better value than all competitors; (2) assume existence of a solution and then analyze its necessary properties to identify it. The former is more direct; the latter is conditional on existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer constructive proofs when possible. If using existence-then-characterize, explicitly address the existence step (cannot simply assume it). Historical caution: Riemann used Dirichlet's principle without proving existence and was criticized by Weierstrass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitly verify existence of extrema (compactness & continuity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The existence of a minimum is not automatic; one must show the admissible set and the objective function satisfy conditions (e.g., continuous function on a compact set) to guarantee a solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For plane problems, restrict the movable domain to a large closed disk if values outside are worse; then apply Weierstrass theorem. Identify when domain is non-compact or function non-continuous, and handle accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-existence counterexamples (careful analysis of admissible set)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are natural-looking extremum problems with no solution because admissible sets are not compact or limit objects violate admissibility (e.g., polygon required to start perpendicular to a line has no shortest admissible path; surfaces constrained to pass through a point may have no minimal-area admissible surface).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples (zigzag polygons, cones approaching disk plus line) to illustrate failure modes. Check closure of admissible set and whether infimum is attained inside the set; if not, only a greatest lower bound exists, not a minimizer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware non-continuous dependence of functionals (length, area)
rubrics_metrics.description: Functionals like curve length are not continuous with respect to naive topologies on curves; sequences of admissible objects may converge to a limit outside the admissible class or change the functional discontinuously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assuming continuity of the objective under limit processes; analyze the topology and compactness of admissible families, and whether limit of minimizing sequence remains admissible. Use appropriate function spaces and compactness criteria in infinite-dimensional settings.
